title: Funds, units and SIPs
blurb: How a pool of money works, why a monthly plan buys more units in a dip, and what fees cost.
t1.title: A pool of money
t1.hook: {people} neighbours each put {each} into one pot. A manager uses the {potTot} to buy small pieces of many companies. Your mission: understand how this pot works.
t1.define: A **mutual fund** pools money from many people. A manager buys many things with it. Each person owns **units** of the pool.
t1.nav: The **NAV** is the price of one unit. It is the fund's total value divided by the number of units.
t1.analogy: A thali holds small portions of many dishes, not one big plate of one dish. A fund holds small pieces of many things.
q1.opt.a: A pool of many people's money, managed to buy many things
q1.opt.b: A loan you give to one company
q1.opt.c: A savings plan with a guaranteed return
q1.opt.d: One share of a single company
q1.fb.c: No fund can guarantee a return. Its value moves with what it holds.
q1.hint: Think of the pot the neighbours filled together.
q1.explain: A mutual fund pools many people's money so a manager can buy many things.
q2.prompt: A fund holds {pool} in total and has issued {units} units. What is the NAV, the price of one unit? Type a number in rupees.
q2.hint: Total value divided by the number of units.
q2.explain: {pool} divided by {units} units is {nav} for one unit.
q3.prompt: At that NAV, how many units does {buyAmt} buy? Type a number.
q3.hint: Your money divided by the price of one unit.
t2.title: A little every month
t2.define: A **SIP** puts the same amount into a fund every month. When the price is low, the same money buys more units. When it is high, it buys fewer.
t2.explore: Open the lab. It starts with four monthly prices and the same amount each month. Drag the prices and watch the units change.
q4.prompt: In the lab, with the starting prices, how many units does the month 2 payment buy? Type a number.
q4.hint: Read the second bar in the lab.
q4.explain: {sipAmt} divided by {nav2} is {u2} units. That is more than in a dearer month.
q5.prompt: How many units in total do the four months buy? Type a number.
q5.explain: The four months buy {u1}, {u2}, {u3} and {u4} units. Together that is {uTotal} units.
q6.prompt: Why does a SIP buy more units when the price falls?
q6.opt.a: The same rupees are divided by a lower price
q6.opt.b: A SIP always makes a profit
q6.opt.c: The manager adds extra units for free
q6.fb.b: A SIP cannot promise a profit. It only spreads your buying over time.
q6.hint: Money divided by a smaller price gives a bigger number.
q6.explain: The same money divided by a lower price gives more units.
t3.title: Fees add up
t3.define: Every fund takes a yearly fee called the **expense ratio**. It comes out of your money every year, so it compounds against you, like interest in reverse.
t3.explore: Open the lab. Set the years to {yrs}, the lower fee to {feeLow} and the higher fee to {feeHigh}. Watch the gap.
q7.prompt: In the lab, what does the higher fee cost you after {yrs} years? Type a number in rupees.
q7.hint: Read the red box under the lab.
q7.explain: On {putIn} put in, the lower fee ends at {netLow} and the higher fee at {netHigh}. The gap is {gap}.
q8.prompt: A fund charges a higher fee than another. What does that tell you?
q8.opt.a: It costs you more every year, and nothing promises better results
q8.opt.b: It will earn more for you
q8.fb.b: A higher fee is only a higher cost. It does not promise a better result.
q8.hint: Look at what the red box in the lab shows.
q8.explain: A fee is a cost. A higher fee does not buy a promise of better results.
t4.title: Kinds of funds
t4.define: An **index fund** follows a list of companies and usually costs less. An **active fund** tries to beat that list and usually costs more. A sector fund holds one industry.
t4.tradeoff: Which suits you depends on how long you can wait, how much you will add, and what it costs. No fund is best for everyone.
q9.prompt: Which statement fits an index fund?
q9.opt.a: It follows a list of companies and usually costs less
q9.opt.b: It promises to beat every other fund
q9.hint: Reread the first card of this task.
q9.explain: An index fund follows a list of companies, so it usually costs less than an active fund.
q10.prompt: Asha asks which fund is the best one. What is a good reply?
q10.opt.a: None is best for everyone. It depends on time, amounts and cost
q10.opt.b: The one with the highest return last year
q10.opt.c: The one with the highest fee
q10.opt.d: Index funds are always the best
q10.fb.b: Last year's winner may not repeat. Past results do not promise future ones.
q10.fb.c: A higher fee is only a higher cost, not a sign of quality.
q10.fb.d: No kind of fund is always best. It depends on your time, your amounts and the cost.
q10.explain: No fund is best for everyone. The right one depends on time, amounts and cost.
q11.prompt: Asha's SIP has run for 3 months and is down a little. What is true?
q11.opt.a: A SIP can lose money. It only spreads the buying over time
q11.fb.b: No plan removes the risk. A SIP spreads your buying, but the units can still be worth less.
q11.hint: Remember what a SIP does, and what it cannot promise.
q11.explain: A SIP spreads buying over time. It cannot guarantee a profit.
glossary.mutual_fund.def: A pool of many people's money, managed to buy many things.
glossary.nav.def: The price of one unit: total value divided by units.
glossary.unit.def: One slice of a fund's pool. You own units of the fund.
glossary.sip.def: Putting the same amount into a fund every month.
glossary.expense_ratio.def: The yearly fee a fund takes out of your money.
glossary.index_fund.def: A fund that follows a list of companies.
